summary: Specifies how to find authoritative RADIUS servers for a given realm using DNS, for use with RADIUS over TLS or DTLS. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of keeping a hand-written list of who to ask, a lookup finds the right server for your organization.

questions: what is radius dynamic peer discovery
how does radius find a server for a realm
what is the nairealm certificate field
subtitle: How a RADIUS server finds the right peer for a user's realm by looking it up in DNS, and checks that the peer is allowed to speak for that realm.

tldr.problem: RADIUS peers must be configured by hand, which becomes unmanageable in a roaming consortium with many realms and servers that change often.
tldr.mechanism: A forwarding server takes the realm from the user name, looks up S-NAPTR (or SRV) records in DNS to find RADIUS/TLS or RADIUS/DTLS servers, then checks the server's X.509 certificate against the realm using a new NAIRealm name.
tldr.outcome: Servers can find each other without a static hierarchy or a central clearinghouse, but it is an Experimental document aimed at roaming consortia that agree on one set of options.

today: RFC 7585 is an Experimental RFC, and no RFC in its metadata obsoletes or updates it. The text itself expects it to be replaced by a Standards Track version once enough experience has been gathered.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Peers Need Discovery
sections.content:
Every transport of RADIUS (UDP, TCP, TLS and DTLS) needs all peers to be configured manually. In a roaming consortium, users are told apart by the realm, which is the part of the Network Access Identifier (NAI, RFC 7542) to the right of the @. With many realms and forwarding servers, one large configuration file is hard to keep up to date, especially when branches add or change realms on their own.

A hierarchy of RADIUS servers organised by top-level domain can help, but it does not always fit. The RFC gives a real deployment organised by country, where a generic domain such as .edu does not map to those borders (see RFC 7593). This document instead stores realm-to-server mappings in DNS, so requests can be forwarded without a static hierarchy.

It also specifies how to check that the server found in DNS is authorised, because an outsider could edit its own DNS records to answer for someone else's realm.
sections.plainLanguage: A giant hand-written list of who runs which server is hard to keep up to date. A shared directory is easier, as long as you can tell the answers are honest.

sections.title: DNS Records and Tags
sections.content:
Servers are published as S-NAPTR records (RFC 3958) or SRV records. If both exist, S-NAPTR results are preferred.

The document defines three S-NAPTR service tags: aaa+auth for authentication (RFC 2865), aaa+acct for accounting (RFC 2866) and aaa+dynauth for dynamic authorization (RFC 5176). It defines two protocol tags: radius.tls.tcp for RADIUS over TLS and radius.dtls.udp for RADIUS over DTLS. The dot in a protocol tag is only a separator for readers and MUST NOT be parsed. For SRV, the labels are _radiustls._tcp and _radiusdtls._udp.

Usually the record label is the DNS A-label form of the realm name. A consortium may instead agree on a different name mapping or service tag. One example in the RFC is a consortium that uses the tag x-eduroam to keep its closed service apart from general-purpose RADIUS.
sections.plainLanguage: Each organisation puts a sign in the directory that says 'for login questions about us, ask this machine, this way'. The tags are the words on the sign.

sections.title: The Realm-to-Server Resolution Algorithm
sections.content:
Discovery is used only when a server gets a request for a realm it is not authoritative for and has no configured next hop. It applies to new user sessions: the first Access-Request, the first accounting packet and the first dynamic authorization packet of a session. Later messages reuse the existing connection.

The input is the User-Name of the form user@realm, where the last @ is the separator. For dynamic authorization it is the operator's domain name from the Operator-Name attribute. In outline, the server takes the realm, applies any consortium name mangling, converts it to a form the resolver can use, and runs a NAPTR query. If NAPTR records with the right service tags exist, it resolves them as RFC 3958 describes. Otherwise it prefixes the realm with _radiustls._tcp. and/or _radiustls._udp. and does an SRV lookup, finally resolving host names to A or AAAA addresses.

The result is a set of host, port, protocol, order and Effective TTL values, plus a backoff time if nothing was found. Three variables have defaults: DNS_TIMEOUT of 3 seconds, MIN_EFF_TTL of 60 seconds and BACKOFF_TIME of 600 seconds. The Effective TTL is the larger of MIN_EFF_TTL and the smallest DNS TTL involved, which avoids thrashing connections. If a result contains the server's own listening address, the algorithm aborts and logs an error, to avoid forwarding loops. While the Effective TTL has not expired, new sessions for that realm SHOULD reuse the open connection.

On retry, only errors that give an immediate response may be retried. A timeout or no reply for more than one second during connection setup counts as a failure, and the next target is tried.
sections.plainLanguage: The server looks at the part of your name after the @, asks the directory who handles that name, and tries the answers in order. If the directory is too slow, it gives up and waits before trying again.

sections.title: Checking That the Server Is Authorised
sections.content:
Discovery does not set up keying material, so TLS pre-shared key ciphersuites cannot be used; only X.509 certificate ciphersuites work. Even with DNSSEC, the server must still prove it is allowed to serve the realm.

The mandatory-to-implement mechanism has two steps. First the certificate is validated as in RFC 5280 and checked to come from a trusted root. Second, the realm value is compared with the server certificate's subjectAlternativeName:otherName:NAIRealm values. A new NAIRealm name form is defined (object identifier id-on-naiRealm, a UTF8String of 1 to 255 characters). It holds an NAI realm and MAY replace the leftmost label with a single asterisk character as a wildcard. The comparison is byte by byte, and a match on any value means authorised.

Two other mechanisms are described. Trust roots plus a configured Policy OID is weaker, because one OID covers every member of the consortium and cannot express authority for one realm. The DNSSEC/DANE approach puts TLSA records for authorised servers in a consortium-agreed DNSSEC zone, and is described as unimplemented. The RFC advises dedicated trust stores, with clients SHOULD start with an empty CA list that administrators add to manually.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding the address is not enough, like finding a phone number in a book. The server also shows an ID badge that says it may speak for that organisation, and the caller checks the badge.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Without DNSSEC on all NAPTR, SRV and A/AAAA replies, the discovery result cannot be trusted. Even with it, authorisation must still be checked using one of the mechanisms above. Because lookups are driven by user input, an attacker could craft a slow DNS zone to cause denial of service. Implementations SHOULD rate limit new executions or pending DNS queries, and MAY lower DNS_TIMEOUT. A server that enables discovery may need to open its address and port to the whole Internet, so it shares the usual attack vectors of TLS services, and failed connection attempts from outsiders still cost computation.

On privacy, classic RADIUS through statically configured clearinghouses lets on-path observers and the clearinghouse see details such as User-Name, which allows mobility profiles. With dynamic discovery, clients can connect directly to the home server, which can remove clearinghouses and reduce the number of intermediaries. The cost is that DNS queries carry the realm name, so observers on the path to DNS servers can learn that a user of that realm tried to authenticate. Because discovery works hop by hop, a hop using RADIUS/UDP weakens the privacy benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can type a made-up name and make the server do lookups, so the server must not wait forever and must limit how many it does. Looking things up in the directory also tells watchers which organisations are being asked about.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Scope
sections.content:
This is an Experimental RFC for roaming consortia that use RADIUS. Its length is undetermined. When enough experience has been gathered on the choice points, it is expected to be obsoleted by a Standards Track version that trims down the options. The base approach, NAPTR records in domains matching NAI realms, is similar to the Diameter approach (RFC 6733), but this document adds authority checking for servers, much more guidance on DNS timeouts and TTLs, and partial detection of routing errors.

Parties that choose different options may not interoperate, and the RFC says global interoperability is not the goal. A consortium's roaming agreement must instead include a profile of which choice points to use, and per-consortium interoperability is the intended scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a trial, meant for groups that agree up front on which options to use. A simpler final version is expected later once people learn what works.
